clinical_scenario: A patient with amyloid-positive (PET) mild AD dementia, no anticoagulation, <=4 cerebral microhemorrhages on MRI is APOE e3/e4. Which treatment is most appropriate?
rationale: Confirmed amyloid early symptomatic AD without ARIA contraindications is an appropriate anti-amyloid candidate with scheduled MRI monitoring.

clinical_scenario: A patient with amyloid-positive mild AD dementia on chronic anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation is APOE e4/e4. Which treatment is most appropriate?
rationale: Concurrent anticoagulation markedly raises ARIA-related hemorrhage risk; anti-amyloid mAbs are generally avoided and symptomatic therapy is appropriate.

clinical_scenario: A patient with amyloid-positive MCI due to AD with MRI showing >4 cerebral microhemorrhages is APOE e3/e3. Which treatment is most appropriate?
rationale: More than four microhemorrhages or prior macrohemorrhage are AUC exclusions for anti-amyloid mAbs due to ARIA-H risk.

clinical_scenario: A patient with moderate-to-severe AD dementia (MMSE 12) is APOE e3/e3. Which treatment is most appropriate?
rationale: Anti-amyloid mAbs are indicated only for MCI / mild AD dementia; memantine is appropriate for moderate-to-severe disease.

clinical_scenario: A patient with mild AD dementia with symptomatic bradycardia and sick sinus syndrome is APOE e3/e4. Which treatment is most appropriate?
rationale: Cholinesterase inhibitors increase vagal tone and can worsen bradycardia or cause syncope; memantine avoids cholinergic cardiac effects.

clinical_scenario: A patient with amyloid-positive (PET) MCI due to AD, no cerebral microhemorrhages, not on anticoagulation, adequate renal and hepatic function is APOE e3/e3. Which treatment is most appropriate?
rationale: Amyloid-confirmed MCI due to AD without ARIA risk factors is an appropriate anti-amyloid antibody candidate per AUC; donanemab is indicated for MCI/mild AD dementia.

clinical_scenario: A patient with amyloid-positive MCI due to AD on chronic oral anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation is APOE e4/e4. Which treatment is most appropriate?
rationale: APOE e4 homozygosity combined with anticoagulation substantially elevates ARIA-related hemorrhage risk; AUC favors symptomatic cholinesterase-inhibitor therapy over anti-amyloid mAb initiation in this combination.

clinical_scenario: A patient with amyloid-positive (PET) mild AD dementia with 3 punctate cerebral microhemorrhages on MRI, no anticoagulation is APOE e3/e4. Which treatment is most appropriate?
rationale: AUC permits anti-amyloid antibody initiation with up to four microhemorrhages absent anticoagulation, with more frequent monitoring MRIs during the titration phase.

clinical_scenario: A patient with amyloid-positive mild AD dementia with a prior lobar intracerebral hemorrhage consistent with cerebral amyloid angiopathy is APOE e3/e3. Which treatment is most appropriate?
rationale: A prior macrohemorrhage, particularly CAA-related, is an AUC exclusion for anti-amyloid antibody therapy given high recurrent ARIA-H risk; symptomatic cholinesterase-inhibitor therapy is appropriate instead.

clinical_scenario: A patient with amyloid-positive (PET) MCI due to AD, no microhemorrhages, on low-dose aspirin only (no anticoagulant) is APOE e2/e3. Which treatment is most appropriate?
rationale: The e2 allele confers comparatively low ARIA risk, and single-agent antiplatelet therapy (unlike anticoagulation) is not an AUC contraindication to anti-amyloid antibody initiation.
